sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Meta's crawling clause, five weeks of publisher pushback, and why newsrooms should answer with machine-readable terms of their own.
sections.para: Meta's updated Commercial Terms, effective 20 November, let it crawl, cache and keep pulling the websites tied to any business using its products, which covers almost every news site. Meta removed 'train' and moved the date, but robots.txt is not in the contract. Letters and regulators are needed; publishers should also state machine-readable terms, price crawls and own their channels.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Eight lines: the terms, the clause, the scope, two moves by Meta, the unchanged core, the response, what to do, what exists.
sections.para: The updated terms cover any business use of Meta's products from 20 November. One clause lets Meta crawl business websites and pull updates. Almost every news organisation has a Page. Meta removed 'train' and moved the date, but robots.txt is not in the contract and saying no means leaving. Publishers should add machine-readable terms, crawl prices, signatures and owned channels.

sections.label: What Tami Hoffman is pointing at
sections.line: The Guardian's Director of Public Policy explains the clause in a 90-second video filling inboxes.
sections.para: Tami Hoffman, Director of Public Policy at The Guardian, posted on 27 October that Meta's update has news organisations around the world riled, and explained why in 90 seconds. The video puts the clause on screen word by word, and shows Meta's page with the paragraph highlighted inside the section where a business grants Meta its licences.

sections.label: The clause, part by part
sections.line: The clause, part by part: who, with what, to do what, where, how often, for what, and the price of saying no.
sections.para: Meta, or anyone acting for it, may use crawlers and create test credentials to access, cache and collect sites tied to a business, and pull updates periodically, for advertising and business products. Checking ad landing pages is a fair use of a crawler. But 'business products' is undefined, robots.txt is not in the text, and refusing means stopping all business use.

sections.label: Five weeks of it
sections.line: Five weeks: 'train' removed, publishers' letters and complaints, the date moved from 30 October to 20 November.
sections.para: The first version allowed content to train Meta's products from 30 October. The News/Media Alliance and the News Media Association objected; Meta removed 'train' and said robots.txt still counts. Open letters, complaints to the Commission and the CMA, and WAN-IFRA's five demands followed. Meta moved the date to 20 November; publishers called it a pause, not a solution.

sections.label: What publishers are asking for
sections.line: WAN-IFRA's five demands: suspend for news, protect paywalls, bind robots.txt, license AI use, decline without losing the tools.
sections.para: WAN-IFRA's president: journalism is not raw material to be collected as a condition of being on a platform. It asks Meta to suspend the clause for news, drop test credentials, make robots.txt binding, exclude unlicensed AI use, and let publishers decline without losing business tools. Four of the five ask Meta to write into the contract what it already says in public.

sections.label: My view: do not only write letters
sections.line: Letters are defensive; publishers should also state, in machine-readable form, what their journalism costs to use.
sections.para: Most demands can be met without waiting: RSL 1.0 states licence terms per use beside robots.txt; Cloudflare's pay per crawl answers crawlers with a price; CC-Signed makes provenance a licence condition; a meter can charge agents as it charges readers; signed, original journalism is what is worth paying for; and owned channels make a platform one door, not the house.

sections.label: How a crawler can behave
sections.line: We crawl too: the PHP story site's source watch runs under written rules, with licence tiers, hashes and an opt-out.
sections.para: The PHP story site's researcher watches 1,330 public pages under written rules: each site's terms and robots.txt followed, a licence tier for every page, A keep and show, B at most 25 words and a link, C link only, captures private with hashes public, and an opt-out in the shared research design. The difference is the rules, and who wrote them.

sections.label: What to watch before 20 November
sections.line: Before 20 November: the text, the regulators, whether publishers leave, and whether any publishes its own terms.
sections.para: Watch whether Meta changes the text and not only the date, adding robots.txt, an exclusion for news or a definition of business products; what the European Commission and the CMA do with requests for interim measures; whether publishers leave Meta's business tools or accept under protest; and whether any publisher answers with machine-readable terms of its own.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: The video is quoted from screenshots, the final text may differ, the timeline is from press reports, and this is not legal advice.
sections.para: The video's spoken explanation is not transcribed here, only what the screenshots show. The clause is quoted as Meta's page and the video show it; the text on 20 November may differ. The timeline comes from press reports of letters and statements. Legal readings are those quoted. The newsroom's own mechanisms are small and partly proposed.

sections.para: Tami Hoffman's post and video as screenshots; Meta's Commercial Terms and update pages; Press Gazette, Engadget, Unite.ai, InPublishing for WAN-IFRA's letter, PPC Land and Nieman Lab for the dispute and the Commission's statement; the RSL 1.0 standard; Cloudflare's pay per crawl; and related newsroom articles on originals, sources, research, signing and ownership.
